support_text: Patient C, a 37-year-old male with acute exacerbation of dermatomyositis/polymyositis, was initially treated with high dose prednisone, methotrexate (MTX) 15 mg/wk im, and cyclosporine 4 mg/kg/day. MTX was suspended after a month's time because of hepatotoxicity, while cyclosporine was suspended after 2 weeks for renal failure and arterial hypertension and prednisone was tapered. Thus the hepatotoxicity that led to MTX discontinuation is attributed to methotrexate.
condition_review: MTX given intramuscularly weekly; passage does not establish depot formulation.

support_text: The paper reports niacin-induced liver injury in humans, describing histopathologic features including necrosis, cholestasis, fibrosis, and hepatocyte vacuolization (Table 2), and presents a case of fatal anicteric acute liver failure with diffuse microvesicular hepatic steatosis due to ER or SR niacin, concluding this scenario may be underrecognized. Time-release (SR) niacin is linked to dose-dependent serum aminotransferase elevations in up to 52% of patients, typically with symptoms above 2 g/day and onset from as early as 2 days to months of exposure.
condition_review: Niacin ER/SR formulation; this is not evidence of long-acting injection.

support_text: Case 3: Chloramphenicol-induced liver injury complicated with systemic allergy (skin rash, fever, leucocytosis and eosinophilia). The liver specimen showed centrolobular necrosis with inflammatory reactions. A challenge test by intramuscular injection of 1 g chloramphenicol caused similar changes and consumed the chloramphenicol antibody (titer dropping from 256:1 to 16:1).
condition_review: Intramuscular chloramphenicol rechallenge; distinguish route and re-exposure from depot formulation.

support_text: A small study documented the use of intramuscular Nandrolone phenylopropionate in patients with refractory anaemia, aplastic anaemia and myelofibrosis; hepatotoxicity was not seen in any of the 13 patients, though there was also no improvement in anaemia (Branda 1973).
condition_review: Intramuscular nandrolone phenylopropionate; identify formulation explicitly rather than infer it from injection.

support_text: There were 11 cases of chlorpromazine jaundice (1.4%), 4 male (1.5%) and 7 female (1.3%), in a cohort of patients receiving chlorpromazine therapy. At onset the drug had been given for from sixteen to thirty-three days (mean twenty-two), and daily dosage and total quantity varied widely and were not significant. All patients took the chlorpromazine by mouth, though 5 had started with intramuscular injections for a few days. Jaundice lasted from one to twenty-six weeks, with a mean duration of two weeks when the 2 most severe cases (lasting thirteen and twenty-six weeks) were excluded, and one fatal case occurred.
condition_review: Oral chlorpromazine with initial intramuscular administration in a subset, not established depot exposure.

support_text: Extended-release naltrexone appears to be safe and well tolerated, with no evidence of hepatotoxicity in subjects treated for 18 months and longer. This is an explicit statement that no human hepatotoxicity was observed with long-term extended-release naltrexone use.
condition_review: Explicit extended-release naltrexone; retain formulation and reported long exposure.

support_text: In the 12-month open-label Vivitrol Extension study by Gastfriend et al. (2005), which enrolled 332 patients from a prior Phase III trial, continued 380 mg or 190 mg intramuscular monthly XR-NTX (naltrexone/Vivitrol) treatment with psychosocial support produced continued reduction in heavy drinking and, among placebo-treated patients switched to Vivitrol, a significant reduction in drinking, with no evidence of hepatotoxicity and no increased discontinuation due to adverse events.
condition_review: Explicit monthly intramuscular XR naltrexone; retain formulation.

support_text: The paper reports three patients who developed symptomatic hepatic dysfunction and states that the implication that oxacillin is the agent responsible is warranted. Two of the three had also received thiamylal sodium prior to onset, but barbiturates are not known to cause hepatitis, and none of the other received drugs are known hepatotoxins. All three received oxacillin intravenously, none had preexisting liver disease, blood transfusions, or hepatitis contact; the rapid reversibility of symptoms and abnormal liver function on discontinuation of oxacillin argues for drug-induced hepatitis rather than viral hepatitis.
condition_review: Intravenous oxacillin; no long-acting injectable formulation established.

support_text: Using specified criteria, the authors identified eight cases of oxacillin-associated hepatitis among patients treated with oxacillin; 46 cases remained with normal liver functions during oxacillin therapy and were treated as the control group. Liver function abnormalities were characteristic of hepatocellular injury, with elevated serum transaminases and lactic dehydrogenases in all eight patients, alkaline phosphatase twice normal in only three, and normal bilirubin levels.
condition_review: Passage establishes oxacillin hepatitis but does not establish formulation.
